subject: Private deployment transport selection: framing, trade-offs, and PoC plan
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>
To: Alex Silver <alex.silver@clearpathhealth.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.com>
Date: 2027-06-18T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Private deployment transport selection: framing, trade-offs, and PoC plan

Alex / Clearpath netops team — thanks for the time yesterday. Per our follow-up, I sketched a short comparison of the three common connectivity patterns for Redwood Private (VPC/on‑prem deployments) so we can lock the PoC approach quickly. Attached: arch-diagram-v1.png and a small latency-benchmark.csv with synthetic numbers to set expectations.

TL;DR recommendation: run a short PoC that treats PrivateLink (interface endpoint) as the primary data path for regulated inference traffic and keep a Site-to-Site (S2S) VPN as a hot standby for on‑prem failover and tooling access. VPC Peering is attractive for intra-cloud, low-latency traffic but has administrative and CIDR‑overlap constraints that make it brittle for multitenant enterprise accounts.

Quick comparison (high level):
- VPC Peering
  - Pros: minimal hop count, predictable RTT, no extra proxy. Good when both accounts are in the same cloud and CIDRs do not overlap.
  - Cons: requires route propagation across accounts, broader surface area (peers see entire subnet routes unless you limit via NACLs), no native private endpoint isolation. Not available across cloud providers.

- PrivateLink (Interface Endpoint)
  - Pros: per-service ENIs + security groups; minimizes route exposure (consumer only gets endpoint IPs), works well across accounts/tenants, easier to limit scope and apply SG/NACL controls. Simpler for compliance (less route sharing).
  - Cons: adds an extra hop and ENI attachment; throughput depends on endpoint sizing and broker (some clouds charge per-connection); need endpoint service setup and permissions.

- Site-to-Site VPN (S2S)
  - Pros: supports on‑prem networks, can NAT to avoid CIDR overlap, supports BGP/policy routing for multi-path. Useful as fallback or for admin/mtce plane.
  - Cons: higher jitter/latency vs in-cloud paths, operational churn (IPSec/IKE lifecycle), can complicate egress auditing without careful path design.

Questions for you before we lock PoC:
1) Any CIDR overlap constraints? (If you have overlapping RFC1918 blocks we should avoid peering unless you can renumber.)
2) Required throughput baseline (Mbps) and concurrency targets for inference traffic.
3) Is route injection (peering-level) acceptable to your networking/security team or do they prefer endpoint-level isolation?
4) Any mandatory cryptographic/KMS requirements (FIPS, HSM integration)?

Proposed PoC plan (1–2 weeks):
- Day 0–1: configure PrivateLink service on our side + grant consumer permissions; spin up interface endpoint on Clearpath test VPC.
- Day 2–4: baseline traffic tests (small generator) to capture latency, jitter, and throughput (I'll run the script that produced latency-benchmark.csv).
- Day 5: Configure S2S VPN as failover with BGP or static routes and validate failover scenarios.
- Day 6–7: run an access audit with your security team and produce a short runbook (mop-poc-checklist.pdf).

If we get a green light on PrivateLink from netops/security, this approach minimizes blast radius while giving you a tested fallback path. If you need absolute lowest one‑way latency for a colocated cloud service, we can pivot to peering with caveats documented.

Next step: can you confirm answers to the four questions above and a 2‑hour window for a joint setup call next week?

Thanks,
Mina Haddad
Senior Solutions Engineer — Redwood Inference

From: Alex Silver <alex.silver@clearpathhealth.com>

Date: 2027-06-18T11:03:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment transport selection: framing, trade-offs, and PoC plan

Mina — thanks, this is helpful. Quick answers:
- CIDR overlap: yes, we have legacy 10.10.0.0/16 in a few sites that we cannot renumber in the PoC window.
- Throughput: baseline 200 Mbps sustained, occasional bursts to 1 Gbps. Concurrency: ~150 active inference sessions.
- Route injection: our security team prefers to avoid broad route sharing — they want the consumer to see only endpoint IPs where possible.
- KMS: must be FIPS‑validated at rest for model artifacts; TLS is fine for transport but we may need HSM-backed key wrapping for some artifacts.

Given those constraints, PrivateLink sounds like a fit (avoid peering). VPN fallback is fine but we need a documented SLA; will your team operate the VPN termination or do you expect us to?

Happy to book a setup call Tuesday morning (PDT).

— Alex
Alex Silver
NetOps Lead, Clearpath Health

From: Connor O'Brien <connor.obrien@redwood.com>
To: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
Cc: Alex Silver <alex.silver@clearpathhealth.com>
Date: 2027-06-18T13:25:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Private deployment transport selection: framing, trade-offs, and PoC plan

Looping in a couple of operational notes from the infra/network side:
- CIDR overlap: since Clearpath cannot renumber 10.10.0.0/16, peering is effectively off the table for the PoC unless Clearpath can NAT or we deploy an intermediate transit VPC with SNAT. That adds complexity.
- PrivateLink behavior: consumer VPC gets an ENI per AZ with private IPs; traffic is NAT'd to the service side (depends on cloud). That matches Alex's ask to avoid route injection and minimizes exposure. Make sure Clearpath's security groups allow the endpoint IPs — we'll provide the ENI prefix list.
- Throughput: some clouds throttle single-ENI throughput; if you need 1 Gbps bursts we should test with multiple concurrent endpoint connections or use a scaled endpoint fleet on our side.
- VPN ops: we can operate VPN termination on our side (managed terminations) and provide a documented runbook. For BGP peering we'll want ASNs and a maintenance window. If Clearpath prefers to host the termination, we can provide the configs and support.

Operational recommendation: PoC = PrivateLink as primary path + S2S VPN termination managed by Redwood as standby. Configure aggressive monitoring and an automatic failover test (1x/day) to validate path health. For the go‑forward deployment we can evaluate adding a peering path later if they renumber.

Connor O'Brien
Network Reliability Engineer, Redwood Inference

Thanks Alex / team — that's perfect and confirms the direction. Action items I will own:
- Send the ENI prefix list and required SG rules (today EOD).
- Provision PrivateLink service and share the service name/ARN; ask you to create the interface endpoint on your side.
- Spin up a small multi-AZ endpoint fleet and run the baseline generator to validate sustained 200 Mbps with burst tests to 1 Gbps; we'll capture 95/99 latencies and jitter for your review.
- Stand up a managed Redwood VPN termination and provide configs (we'll include both static and BGP options).

Proposed meeting: Tue 2027-06-22 09:30–11:30 PDT — setup call + live test window. I will circulate a brief agenda and a Zoom invite. If that works, I'll create the HubSpot engagement HS-83421 and attach the PoC checklist.

Notes for the record: given the regulatory constraints and the need to avoid route injection, PrivateLink primary + managed VPN standby keeps the smallest attack surface while giving you a tested recovery mode. We'll also include our KMS compliance notes for the storage keys used in the PoC.

Thanks — talk soon.
